title: 1. The Sky Mystery
text: Have you ever looked up at the sky and watched an eagle glide effortlessly? No engines, no fuel, just floating in the air! How do they do it while we stay stuck on the ground?

title: 2. Socratic Thinking: Flapping Arms
text: Think about this: If you stick your arms out and flap them really fast, will you fly? Why do you think a small sparrow can fly, but a strong human cannot? Is it just about having wings?

content.title: Inside a Bird's Body
content.description: Notice how a bird's bone is hollow like a pipe, making it super light, while a human bone is solid and heavy.

title: 4. The Reveal: Hollow Bones & Feathers
text: Birds have a secret! Their bones are hollow (filled with air), making them incredibly light. They also have special flight feathers that catch the wind like a parachute. These two things make flying possible.

content.definition: Bones that have empty space inside them, making them lightweight but strong.

content.title: Myth Buster: Feathers
content.text: Many people think feathers are just for flying. Actually, birds have different types of feathers! Down feathers are fluffy and keep them warm, while stiff flight feathers help them fly.

question: Why do birds have hollow bones?
options: To make their bodies lightweight for flying

content.title: 6. Reflection Time
content.text: Explain in your own words: If an elephant suddenly grew feathers and wings, would it be able to fly? Why or why not?

title: 7. Connection: Nature's Airplanes
text: Did you know the first airplanes were invented by studying how birds fly? The shape of an airplane's wing is curved just like a bird's wing to lift it into the air. This is a perfect example of humans copying nature's brilliant design!

content.text: Bring a small empty pipe (like a straw) and a solid stick of the same size to class. Let students feel the weight difference to understand hollow bones.

content.title: 8. Mastery Challenge: Paper Engineer
content.text: Paper Airplane Challenge: Fold a paper airplane. Try adding 'flaps' to the back of the wings by folding them up. Does it fly higher or fall faster? You are now an aerospace engineer!

title: 1. Hook: Hands-Free Tools
text: Imagine trying to crack open a tough walnut without using your hands. Impossible, right? Yet, birds don't have hands, but they can crack nuts, tear meat, and even sew leaves together! How do they do it?

title: 2. Socratic Thinking: The Right Tool
text: If you want to drink juice, you use a straw. If you want to eat soup, you use a spoon. If a bird wants to catch a fish underwater, what shape should its mouth be?

content.title: Beaks as Tools
content.description: Watch how a woodpecker's beak acts like a chisel, while a duck's beak acts like a strainer.

title: 4. The Reveal: Built-In Tools
text: A bird's beak (or bill) is specially shaped for the food it eats! A woodpecker has a strong, chisel-like beak for drilling into wood. An eagle has a sharp, hooked beak for tearing meat. A hummingbird has a long, thin beak like a straw to sip nectar from flowers.

content.definition: The hard, pointed part of a bird's mouth, used for eating, grooming, and building nests. It works like a built-in tool.

question: Which tool is a duck's flat, broad beak most like?
options: A strainer used in the kitchen

content.title: 6. Reflection Time
content.text: Why doesn't a sparrow, which eats small seeds, have a long sharp beak like a woodpecker?

title: 7. Connection: Adapting to the Environment
text: Animals change over thousands of years to survive where they live. A bird's beak tells us the story of its home and its diet. This is called 'Adaptation', a major idea discovered by scientists by looking at nature!

content.title: 8. Mastery Challenge: Bird Watcher
content.text: Bird Watcher Challenge: Look outside your window for 10 minutes. Find one bird, look closely at its beak, and try to guess what it eats based on the shape!
